cards.name: Order form / checkout copy
cards.summary: The words on the order page, cart and checkout: they restate exactly what the buyer gets, show the full price once, answer the last doubts (delivery, returns, payment safety) and label every field and button so nobody stalls. Good checkout copy is short, specific and honest; it removes reasons to leave rather than adding persuasion.
use_for: Order page at the end of a sales page or VSL (course, coaching, info product)
Shopify / WooCommerce cart and checkout text for D2C brands (cart drawer, shipping line, COD note)
Order bumps and one-click upsell boxes
Payment-step microcopy: UPI / card / COD choices, error and declined-payment messages
Subscription sign-up step (what renews, when, how to cancel)
avoid: Re-selling the whole product on the order page: one recap block, then get out of the way; long persuasion belongs in genre:sales_page
General app or SaaS interface text outside the purchase path: use genre:ux_microcopy
Recovering people who already left: that is genre:abandoned_cart_email
Any countdown, stock counter or pre-ticked add-on that is not literally true or opt-in (dark patterns under comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023)

sources.title: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023
sources.supports: bans false urgency, confirm shaming, drip pricing, basket sneaking, trick questions, nagging, subscription traps on platforms selling in India

sources.title: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements, 2022
sources.supports: claims must be capable of substantiation; 'free' only when the consumer pays nothing beyond unavoidable cost; disclaimers may clarify but not contradict the claim

buyers: D2C brands on Shopify or WooCommerce
Course creators and coaches selling through a sales page
cards.value_why: AWAI's 2026 project list names 'Order Page/Shopping Cart Sequence' as its own copywriting project, but it is almost always sold inside a sales-page or funnel package, not alone. The leverage is real: Baymard's checkout research (updated 2025-09-22) puts documented cart abandonment at 70.22%, and most of the top reasons (extra costs, trust, forced account, unclear total) are copy and disclosure problems.
cards.goal: The buyer completes payment without leaving to check something, and is not surprised by anything on the confirmation page or the bank statement.

structure.does: Restates the offer in the buyer's words so they know they are in the right place: product, quantity or plan, and the main result.
Lists each item or module once with its plain description (and value only if the value is real). Matches the sales page exactly, same names.
Shows the total the buyer will actually pay, once, with GST, delivery and any COD fee already inside it or listed right under it. Subscriptions state the renewal amount and date.
States the guarantee or return/refund terms in one concrete sentence: how many days, what the buyer does, what they get back.
Answers the payment and delivery doubts: accepted methods (UPI, cards, COD), secure payment partner, dispatch time, support contact.
Plain labels outside the box, helper text only where people get it wrong (PIN code, GSTIN, phone for delivery updates). Says why you need any unusual field.
Verb plus what happens, with the amount where it helps: 'Pay Rs 1,299 and place order'. Never 'Submit'.
One relevant add-on, unticked by default, with its price and one reason it belongs with this order.
Under the button or on the thank-you step: when the confirmation arrives, where (email, WhatsApp), when it ships or when access opens.

length.note: Whole visible page text excluding the product names in the cart. Low-price D2C checkouts sit near 60-120 words; high-ticket course order pages with a bump and guarantee run 180-300. Every extra line must answer a doubt.

checklist: Does the headline name the exact product, plan or quantity the buyer chose?
Do item names in the recap match the sales page word for word?
Is the full payable total (with GST, delivery and any COD fee) visible before the payment step?
For a subscription, are the renewal amount, renewal date and how to cancel stated next to the button?
Does the guarantee say the number of days and what the buyer has to do?
Is every add-on unticked by default and priced?
Is the button label a verb plus outcome, not 'Submit' or 'Continue'?
Is any urgency (deadline, seats, stock) literally true and checkable?
Is the marketing opt-in a separate, unticked checkbox rather than bundled into the purchase?
Does the page say what happens after payment and where the confirmation will arrive?
pitfalls: Drip pricing: the Rs 999 on the product page becomes Rs 1,248 at the last step after a 'convenience fee'. Baymard's top abandonment reason is extra costs; India's dark-pattern guidelines ban drip pricing. Show the full total on the first checkout screen.
Pre-ticked order bumps or 'protection plans' added to the cart: basket sneaking under comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023. Leave the box empty and let the one-line reason sell it.
Confirm-shaming decline links ('No thanks, I like paying full price'): banned as confirm shaming. Write a neutral 'No, continue to payment'.
Fake countdown timers that restart on refresh, or 'Only 3 left' that never changes: false urgency. Use a real deadline with its date, or nothing.
Vague guarantees ('100% satisfaction guaranteed!'): say '7-day replacement if the bottle arrives damaged: WhatsApp a photo to 98xxx xxxxx'.
Forcing account creation before payment (an abandonment reason in Baymard's data): offer guest checkout and say 'We'll create your account from this order'.
cards.exemplar_brief: Checkout page copy for a Pune D2C cold-brew coffee brand's Rs 1,299 starter kit (2 cold-brew bottles, 1 glass, recipe card; free delivery; COD Rs 49 extra), buyers arriving from an Instagram ad; English with one Hinglish reassurance line allowed; 120-220 words covering order headline, recap bullets, price block, 7-day damaged-bottle replacement, trust and delivery line, PIN-code helper text, button label and one unticked order bump (extra bottle at Rs 349); goal: the buyer pays by UPI or picks COD without leaving the page.

verified.note: 8/10 (purpose 2, structure 2, specificity 2, voice 1, craft 1). Every briefed part is present in card order: headline naming the kit, recap, price block with a GST-inclusive total and a separate COD total of Rs 1,348, 7-day damaged-bottle replacement saying what the buyer does, UPI/card/COD line, PIN helper, unticked Rs 349 bump with a reason, separate unticked opt-in, amount-led button, what happens next. Placeholders [support WhatsApp number] and [dispatch time] are fair. Fixes: Hinglish gender slip in 'Bottle toot gayi ... naya bottle hum bhejenge' (bottle is feminine: 'nayi bottle'); the delivery form has no address or email field although the confirmation is promised by email; the trust line names no payment partner. Fault: writer (minor).

cards.name: Packaging & label copy
cards.summary: Every word on the pack except the legal panel the client's regulatory team supplies: product name and descriptor, one front-of-pack claim, variant callouts, a short back-of-pack story, usage directions and the care line. Good pack copy is read in seconds on a shelf or a quick-commerce thumbnail, makes only claims the client can prove, and never fights the mandatory declarations for space.
use_for: New food, beverage, personal-care and home-care SKUs from Indian D2C and FMCG brands
Range extensions where variant names and callouts must stay consistent across 3-10 packs
Back-of-pack brand stories and usage instructions
Gift boxes, cartons, sleeves, hang tags and inserts (thank-you cards, QR cards)
Bilingual or regional-language pack versions
avoid: Writing or 'tidying' the mandatory declarations (net quantity, MRP, manufacturer details, ingredients, licence numbers, dates): those come from the client's regulatory or QA team under Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) and FSSAI labelling rules; you leave space for them and never paraphrase them
Online product pages: genre:product_description and genre:marketplace_listing have different jobs and more room
Brand-level manifestos on a 4 cm side panel: one line of story, link the rest with a QR
Health, disease or performance claims the client cannot document: drop them or get them substantiated first

sources.title: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements, 2022
sources.supports: claims must be capable of substantiation; 'free' only when the consumer pays nothing beyond unavoidable cost; disclaimers may clarify but not contradict the claim

sources.title: ASCI Code for Self-Regulation of Advertising Content
sources.supports: every claim about objectively ascertainable fact must be capable of substantiation (Ch I.1); no unfair denigration of competitors (Ch IV)

buyers: D2C food, beauty and home brands
Private-label manufacturers for quick-commerce and modern trade
cards.value_why: Per the PCW harvest, pack copy is usually written by brand agencies inside packaging design projects; no separate freelance market list was found. It is worth taking on as part of a launch package (name, pack copy, listing, A+ content).
cards.goal: A shopper picks this pack over the one next to it, understands what it is and how to use it, and the brand is never asked to prove a claim it cannot.

structure.does: Brand, product name and a plain descriptor that says what is inside ('Cold-pressed groundnut chutney powder'). The descriptor must survive a thumbnail on a quick-commerce app.
The one reason to buy, specific and provable ('Made with Guntur chillies, no added colour'). One claim, not five.
Flavour, strength, size or skin type, plus at most 2-3 short callouts (veg, no added sugar, recyclable) that are true and documented.
Who makes it, why it is different, one concrete sensory or origin detail. Written to be read in the kitchen, not on a pitch deck.
Numbered steps or a single serving suggestion with quantities and times.
How to store after opening, shelf-life note in plain words if the client supplies it, and how to dispose of or recycle the pack.
Space reserved for the declarations the client's regulatory team provides verbatim. You only check that your copy does not contradict them.
Where to reach the brand and what the QR opens (recipe, refill, authenticity).

length.note: Copy you write, excluding the supplied mandatory panel and ingredient list. A 50 g sachet carries 25-50 words; a 500 g jar or carton 100-220. Pack size and the number of languages on pack set the ceiling.

checklist: Can a shopper tell what the product is from the name and descriptor alone?
Is there exactly one front-of-pack claim, and does the client hold proof for it?
Is every callout (veg, no added sugar, natural, recyclable) true for this exact SKU and documented?
Is the copy free of absolutes like 'chemical-free', 'no side effects' or 'India's best'?
Are usage steps numbered with quantities and times?
Does nothing in the brand copy contradict the mandatory panel (weight, ingredients, veg/non-veg mark)?
Do variant names and callout wording match across the whole range?
Has the regional-language version been transcreated and checked by a native reader rather than machine-translated?
Does the QR line say what the scan opens?
pitfalls: 'Chemical-free' or '100% natural' on a product with processing aids or preservatives: an unprovable claim under ASCI's substantiation rule and the CCPA misleading-ads guidelines. Name the specific true fact: 'No added preservatives' or 'Only 4 ingredients'.
Front of pack crammed with six badges: on a shelf or a phone thumbnail none of them reads. Pick one claim; move the rest to the back.
Back-of-pack story that is pure adjectives ('crafted with passion and love'): replace with one detail a stranger can picture: 'Roasted in small batches in our Guntur kitchen every Tuesday'.
Paraphrasing the ingredient list or net quantity to 'make it friendlier': mandatory declarations must stay exactly as the client's regulatory team supplies them.
Hindi line produced by machine translation ('Yeh aapke swasthya ke liye uttam hai'): transcreate to how a buyer actually speaks, and have a native reader check spelling and matras before print.
Writing before seeing the dieline: ask for the dieline and panel sizes first, then budget words per panel.
cards.exemplar_brief: Front and back pack copy for a 200 g jar of cold-pressed groundnut chutney powder (podi) from a Guntur family brand selling on Blinkit and Amazon; audience: urban home cooks aged 25-40 outside Andhra; English front panel with a Hindi usage line on the back; 80-160 words excluding the mandatory panel and ingredient list (client supplies both); one front claim, two callouts, a 50-word origin story, three usage suggestions; goal: the shopper picks it over the default masala and knows how to use it the first day. Client facts (demo data for this test; brand invented): brand Venkata Pantry, product Groundnut Podi, 200 g. Front claim the client can prove (production records): cold-pressed groundnuts, ground in small 40 kg batches. The two callouts it can document (lab report on file): 'No added colour' and 'No preservatives'. The veg mark and ingredient list sit on the supplied panel (groundnuts 48%, Guntur red chilli 30%, garlic 12%, rock salt 6%, cumin 4%). Origin: started in 1987 in Kanakamma's kitchen in Guntur; the pressed groundnuts are dry-roasted in an iron kadhai, the chillies sun-dried for three days, everything stone-ground. Usage: 1 tsp mixed into hot rice with ghee; stirred into sesame oil as a dip for idli or dosa; sprinkled over curd rice. Best before 6 months from packing; keep dry.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Front panel is right: brand, name, plain descriptor, the one provable claim (cold-pressed, 40 kg batches) and the two documented callouts, with space left for the supplied veg mark and ingredients. Origin story (about 55 words) is concrete and ties back to the callout ('the colour you see in the jar is only the chilli's own'); three numbered usage lines plus a natural Hindi first-day line; storage line adds 'use a dry spoon'. Nits (writer): the card's consumer-care/QR line and a disposal or recycling note are missing (a slot would do); opening sentence is clunky ('grew out of ... where it started in 1987'). | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: Personal brand statement
cards.summary: One or two sentences that say who a person helps, with what result, and what makes their way of doing it different, written once and then cut down for the LinkedIn headline, bio first line, portfolio header and spoken intro. Good ones name a specific audience and a specific outcome; weak ones are a stack of adjectives.
use_for: Source line for a LinkedIn headline and About opening
Portfolio or personal-site hero line
Speaker intros, podcast-guest intros and event badges
Freelancer and consultant profiles on marketplaces
Career switchers who need to explain the new direction in one breath
avoid: A full bio with history and credentials: use genre:professional_bio
A whole LinkedIn profile: genre:linkedin_profile builds on this statement
A company's market position: use genre:positioning_statement
A 30-60 second spoken pitch to an investor or buyer: use genre:elevator_pitch

sources.title: Fiverr Writing & Translation: LinkedIn Profiles
sources.supports: personal-branding copy is sold bundled with LinkedIn profile writing

buyers: LinkedIn ghostwriters and resume writers (as a deliverable inside a package)
cards.value_why: Sold inside LinkedIn profile and resume packages rather than alone (Fiverr bundles it with LinkedIn profile writing). It is a small deliverable that decides whether the rest of the package works.
cards.goal: The right person reads it once and knows whether this is someone they should contact, hire or follow.

structure.does: A specific audience defined by role, stage or situation ('D2C founders doing Rs 5-50 crore'), not 'businesses' or 'people'.
The result they get, as a verb and a measurable or visible change ('close GST notices without a penalty').
The one distinctive method, credential or track record that makes the outcome believable ('9 years, 400+ notices handled').
A value, language, region or style that helps the right people self-select ('in Hindi or English').
The same statement shortened for a headline (under about 120 characters), a bio first line and a spoken 'I help...' sentence. Same nouns in all three.

length.note: The master statement. Cut-downs are shorter. Longer than two sentences means it has turned into a bio.

checklist: Does it name a specific audience, not 'businesses', 'brands' or 'people'?
Does it state an outcome the audience wants, as a verb, not a job title?
Is there one concrete proof point (years, count, named result) the person can back up?
Is it free of adjectives the reader cannot verify (passionate, results-driven, dynamic)?
Could a competitor paste it into their own profile unchanged? (It must fail that test.)
Is it two sentences or fewer?
Do the headline and bio cut-downs keep the same audience and outcome words?
pitfalls: 'Passionate, results-driven marketer who loves storytelling': three claims nobody can check. Rewrite as audience + outcome + proof: 'I write launch emails for Indian edtech brands; my last 6 launches averaged 2.1x the previous campaign's revenue.' (Use only numbers the client gives you.)
Listing every service: one audience and one outcome. Other services live in the About section.
Job-title-only statements ('Senior Product Designer at X'): add who that work helps and what changes for them.
Inflated scope ('helping India go digital'): small and true beats big and vague; the reader decides in one glance.
Different nouns on every profile: the person becomes three people. Lock the audience and outcome words and reuse them.
cards.exemplar_brief: Personal brand statement for a Jaipur chartered accountant (9 years in practice, specialises in GST notices and audits for D2C brands, works in Hindi and English); used as the source for her LinkedIn headline, portfolio header and podcast-guest intro; English; master statement under 45 words plus a headline cut under 120 characters and a one-sentence spoken intro; goal: a D2C founder who reads it knows in one glance whether to message her.

verified.note: 8/10 (purpose 2, structure 1, specificity 2, voice 2, craft 1). Specific audience (D2C founders), a verb outcome, the one supplied proof (9 years), the Hindi/English edge, and three cut-downs that keep the same nouns; headline 100 characters; no buzzwords; nothing invented. The master statement leads with the credential instead of the card's who-you-help-first order, and the outcome 'answer GST notices and get through audits with the right papers' is soft (no visible change for the founder). Fault: writer (minor).

cards.name: Personal essay / creative nonfiction
cards.summary: A first-person true story that turns one lived experience into an insight a stranger cares about: scenes first, reflection after, and an ending that is earned by the story rather than announced. It covers literary essays for magazines and anthologies and the creator version (a lesson-led story post that ends on a takeaway).
use_for: Literary and magazine personal essays, anthology submissions and essay contests
Newsletter and Substack essays for creators, founders and professionals
Lesson-led story posts for LinkedIn or Medium (the shorter creator version)
Ghostwritten first-person pieces for a founder or public figure, from interviews
Memoir chapters tested as standalone essays
avoid: Argument-led opinion with a news peg: use genre:opinion_column
Admissions essays with a prompt and word limit: use genre:college_essay or genre:statement_of_purpose
Brand origin stories written for a company page: use genre:brand_story
Diary-style posts with no insight for a stranger: if you cannot say what the reader takes away, the piece is not ready

sources.title: EFA 2026 Rate Chart (member survey Nov 2025-Jan 2026)
sources.supports: Ghostwriting > Articles/essays 15.0-30.0 cents per word, $75-$100 per hour

sources.title: Fiverr: Articles & Blog Posts category (Article type facet read 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: supply signal: First-person narrative 1507 gigs; Long-form article 3494 gigs

sources.title: Reedsy: Find Book Ghostwriting Services
sources.supports: marketplace guide prices for ghostwriting (book ghostwriting average $450 per 1,000 words, 2025; short-form $500-$2,000)

buyers: Magazines, literary journals and anthologies (small fees)
Founders and executives who want a ghostwritten first-person essay
Brands commissioning employee or customer stories (with consent)
cards.value_why: Small paid market (some magazines and anthologies). Rate evidence: EFA 2026 rate chart, Ghostwriting > Articles/essays 15-30 cents per word; Reedsy lists short-form ghostwriting at $500-$2,000. Fiverr shows 1,507 'First-person narrative' gigs on 2026-10-04 (a supply signal, not demand). Its value is rising as a counter to generic AI content, because first-hand experience is the one thing a model cannot supply.
cards.goal: The reader finishes, feels they understood something about their own life through someone else's, and shares or replies.

structure.does: Drops the reader into one specific moment: a place, a time, a person, a line of dialogue or an action. No throat-clearing, no thesis.
Makes clear, lightly, what is at stake for the narrator or what the essay is trying to understand.
Two to four scenes or memories that complicate the question, alternating with short reflection. Each scene adds new information or pressure.
The moment the narrator sees differently: a fact learned, a line someone said, an action that surprises.
What the narrator understands now, stated in concrete terms and reaching beyond the anecdote to the reader's world.
Lands on an image, an action or a callback to the opening, not a moral. Creator version: one clear takeaway line.

length.note: Creator story posts run 300-700 words; newsletter essays 800-2,000; magazine and anthology essays 1,500-4,000. The publication's guidelines decide; check them before drafting.

checklist: Does the first paragraph put the reader inside a specific moment rather than state a theme?
Is there at least one line of dialogue or one exact sensory detail per scene?
Does each middle scene add new information or raise the stakes, rather than repeat the first?
Is there a clear turn where the narrator understands something new?
Is the insight earned by the scenes, not announced before them?
Does the ending avoid a stated moral ('This taught me that...')?
Are real people who could be identified either consenting or disguised (names, details changed) and portrayed fairly?
Is every factual claim (dates, places, numbers) true, since this is nonfiction?
Would the piece still mean something to a reader who has never met the narrator?
pitfalls: Starting with the lesson ('Failure is the best teacher. Let me explain.'): open on the scene and let the reader arrive at the lesson a beat before you state it.
Summary instead of scene ('My father was always strict'): show one moment: 'He timed my homework with the steel wall clock and wrote the minutes in the margin.'
Ending on a moral or a LinkedIn-style 'Agree?': end on an image or action that carries the meaning.

Exposing family members, ex-partners or colleagues without consent: change names and identifying details, and remove anything that is only there to settle a score; true but harmful imputations can still raise defamation questions (comp:bns_defamation_speech).
AI-flavoured filler ('In today's fast-paced world', 'little did I know', 'a journey of self-discovery'): readers of this genre spot it at once; cut it and replace with a specific memory.
Ghostwriting without interviews: a first-person essay needs the subject's own details and phrases. Record a 45-60 minute interview and build from their words.

ban.label: stock essay cliche / AI tell
ban.regex: (?i)in today'?s fast[- ]paced world|little did i know|journey of self[- ]discovery|this taught me (a|an) (valuable|important) lesson|\btapestry\b

cards.exemplar_brief: Personal essay for a Bengaluru fintech product manager's Substack: the week she taught her 68-year-old father in Bhagalpur to pay by UPI after his bank branch shut, told through three scenes (the closed branch, the first failed payment at the sabzi stall, the day he paid the priest by QR); audience: urban professionals with parents in small towns; English with a few untranslated Hindi words; 900-1,200 words; goal: the reader finishes and forwards it to a sibling.

verified.note: 9/10 (purpose 2, structure 2, specificity 2, voice 2, craft 1). Opens inside the scene at the shuttered branch, states the question lightly, runs the three briefed scenes in order with exact sensory detail and natural Hindi dialogue, has a clear turn (the fifth step is trusting the screen), an earned reflection that reaches the reader, and ends on an action (the Rs 1 sent back), not a moral. Deviations: the brief asked for untranslated Hindi words but every Hindi line is glossed in English; the passbook detail is slightly illogical (she carries it to Bengaluru 'in case the new branch needed it'). Reconstructed scene details are correctly flagged for the narrator to confirm.

cards.name: Photo caption / cutline
cards.summary: One or two sentences under a news or editorial photo that tell the reader who is in it, what is happening, where and when, plus one piece of context the picture cannot show, followed by the credit. Good captions are exact (names spelled, people placed left to right) and never describe what the reader can already see.
use_for: News photos in print, web and e-paper editions
Photo galleries and photo essays
Government and NGO press photos sent with a press note
Annual reports, magazines and books with editorial photos
Archive and museum image captions
avoid: Social-media captions written to drive engagement: use genre:instagram_caption
Screen-reader descriptions for accessibility: use genre:alt_text (a caption complements alt text, it does not replace it)
Captions that make a claim the photo does not support (old photo, different place): verify date and place first or do not run it

sources.title: AP Stylebook (official site, subscription)
sources.supports: the style guide most English-language newsrooms follow for captions; the caption conventions in this card (present tense for the action, past tense for context, people named left to right) come from the PCW harvest note, not quoted from the stylebook

sources.title: MeitY: IT Rules amendment G.S.R. 120(E), 10 Feb 2026 (consolidated text)
sources.supports: realistic AI-generated or altered images ('synthetically generated information') must be prominently labelled

buyers: Newspapers, news websites and magazines (photo and copy desks)
cards.value_why: A desk skill bundled into editing and photo-desk roles; no standalone freelance category was found on 2026-10-04 (PCW harvest). Still worth a card because a wrong name or place in a caption is the most visible correction a publication runs.
cards.goal: The reader knows exactly who and what they are looking at, where and when, and learns one fact the photo cannot show.

structure.does: Who (full names and roles, left to right for groups), doing what (present tense), where (specific place) and when (day or date).
Why it matters or what led to it, in past tense: the event, the number, the outcome. Not a description of the image.
Photographer and agency or source, in the publication's credit style. Add 'File photo' with the year for archive images, and an AI label if the image is generated or altered.

length.note: Single news photo: 15-45 words. Lead photos and galleries can take a second context sentence. Credit line counted separately.

checklist: Does it name every identifiable person who matters, with role, left to right?
Are all names spelled as in an official or verified source?
Is the action in present tense and the background in past tense?
Does it give the specific place and the day or date?
Does it add at least one fact the photo cannot show?
Is it free of phrases that describe the obvious ('is seen', 'pictured here', 'in this photo')?
Is an old photo marked 'File photo' with its year?
Is an AI-generated or altered image labelled as such?
Is there a credit line?
pitfalls: Describing the picture ('Devotees are seen standing in water'): the reader can see that. Say who, where and why: 'Devotees offer arghya to the rising sun at Gandhi Ghat, Patna, on Thursday, the last day of Chhath.'
Guessing names from a press release photo: confirm with the organiser or photographer; when unsure, identify by role ('a ward councillor, second from left, who declined to give her name').
Recycled file photos captioned as today's event: say 'File photo, 2023' or find a current image.
Opinion in the caption ('a historic moment', 'a huge crowd'): give the number from a named source instead, or leave it out.
Hindi captions that drop the date or place because the headline has it: the caption must stand alone, since pages are cropped and photos get shared without the story.

ban.label: describes the obvious
ban.regex: (?i)\b(is|are) seen\b|pictured here|\bin this (photo|picture|image)\b|\babove (photo|picture)\b|तस्वीर में देखा जा सकता

cards.exemplar_brief: Caption for a Patna Hindi daily's e-paper: Chhath devotees offering arghya at Gandhi Ghat at sunrise, with three named organisers in the foreground; Hindi in Devanagari; 20-45 words plus a credit line; goal: a reader knows who, what, where and when, and one fact the photo cannot show. Reporter's details (demo data for this test; names invented): morning of Tuesday 28 October 2025 (usha arghya, the last day of Chhath). Organisers left to right: राजेश कुमार सिंह, अध्यक्ष, गांधी घाट छठ पूजा समिति; सुनीता देवी, संयोजक, महिला स्वयंसेवक दल; अरविंद प्रसाद, वार्ड पार्षद. District administration's estimate: about 2.5 lakh devotees along the ghat stretch. Credit: फोटो: रवि शंकर, स्टाफ फोटोग्राफर.

verified.note: 9/10. Idiomatic Hindi news caption: place, event and present-tense identification with 'आगे बाएं से', past-tense attributed crowd estimate as the fact the photo cannot show, separate credit, no 'तस्वीर में'; usha arghya on the last day of Chhath is correct; 45 body words. Names, roles, day and estimate are placeholders only because the brief says the reporter supplied them but supplies none (not penalised). CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> actually give the three organisers' names and roles left to right, the date and weekday, and the district administration's crowd figure, or say 'use placeholders'. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_c): exemplar_brief now gives the three organisers' names and roles left to right, the date and weekday, the administration's crowd figure and the credit; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Pillar page
cards.summary: A broad hub page that covers a core topic at overview depth and links out to every detailed cluster article on it (and gets links back from each). Good pillar pages answer the main question in the first screen, give each subtopic a short self-contained section with a descriptive link to the deep article, and show first-hand expertise that a generic AI summary cannot.
use_for: The hub page of a topic cluster on a B2B, SaaS, finance, health or professional-services site
Restructuring a blog that has 10-40 posts on one topic but no page tying them together
Resource or 'learn' sections (GST for D2C brands, home loans, UPSC preparation)
Category hubs that sit between a service page and detailed guides
avoid: A single long article with no cluster behind it: that is genre:ultimate_guide

structure.does: The best 15-40 seconds of the episode (a guest line, a surprising fact or a question) before any intro music, so the listener knows why to stay.
Show name, host, and the episode's promise in one sentence: what the listener will know or feel by the end.
Who the guest is and why they are the right person for this topic; two specific credentials, not a CV.

Credits, next-episode tease and any disclaimer.

Is the episode's promise stated in one sentence in the intro?
Does every segment have a stated goal and a time estimate?
Are interview questions open (how, why, what happened) with at least one follow-up per main question?
Are ad breaks placed at natural pauses, not mid-story?
Are clip-worthy moments or chapter points marked for the video edit?
Is scripted copy written for the ear (short sentences, no parentheses, no 'as you can see')?
Does the close give one call to action, not three?
Are claims about named people or companies sourced or framed as opinion?

No research on the guest: a good guide quotes the guest's own past interviews or posts and asks what they have not been asked.

cards.goal: The listener or reader feels something specific and remembers at least one line; at an occasion, the people being honoured recognise themselves.

structure.does: A phrase from inside the poem or a concrete image, not a label like 'Anniversary Poem'.
Starts with something the reader can see, hear, smell or touch, in a specific place and time.
Builds through 2-4 more images or moments, each adding something; the occasion version uses the real details from the brief here.
A shift in time, tone, speaker or meaning that makes the reader see the earlier lines differently.
Lands on an image, a repeated line returning changed, or a blessing for occasional verse. It does not explain the poem.
Line breaks at breaths, a refrain the audience can catch, pauses marked for the performer.

length.note: Greeting and social verse: 8-16 lines; occasion readings: 16-30 lines (about 1-3 minutes aloud); spoken-word performance: 30-60 lines. A named form fixes its own line count; follow it exactly.

checklist: Does the poem open on a concrete image rather than an abstract statement?
Is every abstraction (love, time, hope) anchored to a specific object, place or act?
Is there a turn where the meaning or tone shifts?
Does the last line land without explaining the poem?
For occasional verse, are the real names and at least three details from the brief used accurately?
If a form was requested, do the line count, metre and rhyme scheme follow it exactly?
Does it read naturally aloud, with line breaks at breaths?
Is it free of borrowed lines from existing poems or songs?
pitfalls: Abstract greeting-card verse ('Your love is a light that guides my way'): replace with a shared detail: 'the blue Bajaj you sold to pay my school fees'.
Forced rhyme that bends the sense or word order: if the rhyme costs meaning, break it or go free verse.
AI-verse tells ('tapestry', 'symphony of', 'whispers of the wind', 'dance of destiny'): cut them; they mark the poem as generic in one line.
Explaining the poem in the last stanza ('And so we learn that love endures'): end on the image and trust the reader.
Hindi poems with broken matras or mixed scripts by accident: have a native reader check spelling, and decide deliberately between Devanagari and Roman.
Pasting famous lines (Gulzar, Bachchan, Faiz) into a commissioned piece: quote briefly with credit if the client insists, never present them as new work.

cards.name: Policy brief
cards.summary: A short, evidence-based document that tells a decision-maker what to do about a policy problem and why: recommendation first, then the problem, the options and the concrete steps. Good briefs are written for a busy official, not an academic, separate fact from opinion, cite every number, and make the recommended action specific enough to approve.

Briefing notes for ministers, MPs, MLAs and district administrations
Advocacy briefs that accompany a campaign or a research report
Corporate public-policy and government-affairs submissions
Research-to-policy summaries of an academic study
avoid: A long research document with full methods: use genre:research_report or genre:white_paper
An opinion piece for the public: use genre:opinion_column
Explaining an existing scheme to citizens: use genre:scheme_explainer
A party's promises to voters: use genre:election_manifesto

cards.goal: The decision-maker understands the problem in two minutes and approves, schedules or funds the recommended action.

structure.does: States the recommendation or the problem in plain, memorable words ('Ward heat plans can cut heatstroke admissions in Bihar's cities').
Bottom line first: the problem in one sentence, the recommendation, the cost or effort, and the expected result. UNC: one to two paragraphs.

structure.part: Context and scope of the problem
structure.does: Why this needs action now, with 2-5 sourced data points (numbers with year and source) and who is affected where.
Current approach plus 2-3 realistic alternatives, each with cost, feasibility, who implements it and trade-offs, ideally in a table.
Numbered concrete steps: who does what, by when, with what budget or legal instrument, and how success will be measured.
Every number traceable to a named, dated source.
Methods, extra data or case studies that would distract from the main argument.

length.note: Most briefs fit in 2-4 pages. A one-page version for a minister is often requested alongside. The decision-maker's time, not the research volume, decides.

checklist: Does the first paragraph state the recommendation, not just the problem?
Is every number given with its source and year?
Are at least two alternatives compared on cost, feasibility and trade-offs?
Does each recommendation name who acts, what they do and by when?
Is jargon either removed or explained in one clause?
Are fact and the author's judgement clearly separated (attributed data vs 'we recommend')?
Could an official read only the title and summary and know what is being asked?
Is it within the length the audience will read (usually 2-4 pages)?
pitfalls: Academic structure (literature review, methods, findings, then a recommendation on page 9): flip it. Recommendation in paragraph one; methods to the appendix.

Vague asks ('the government should take holistic steps'): write 'The Urban Development Department should notify ward heat action plans in Patna, Gaya and Bhagalpur before 1 March, at an estimated cost of Rs X crore from the existing SDRF allocation' (cost from the client's data).
Unattributed claims ('studies show', 'experts agree'): name the study, the year and the number.
Only one option presented: officials trust a brief that shows it considered alternatives and their downsides.
Ignoring the decision-maker's constraints (budget cycle, legal power, election calendar): say which instrument (order, scheme guideline, budget line) delivers the recommendation.
cards.exemplar_brief: Policy brief from a Patna civic NGO to the Bihar Urban Development and Housing Department recommending ward-level heat action plans for five Tier-2 cities (Gaya, Bhagalpur, Muzaffarpur, Purnia, Darbhanga); audience: the Principal Secretary and district magistrates; English with a one-page Hindi summary; 1,500-2,000 words with an options table; goal: the department schedules a decision meeting on a pilot. NGO data (demo data for this test; all figures invented): IMD district data, average heatwave days per city per season: 6.2 in 2019, 11.4 in 2025. Heatstroke admissions at the five district hospitals: 212 in 2019, 486 in 2025 (+129%). 12-ward pilot survey, n = 1,260 households: 68% had no cool indoor space at midday; of 410 outdoor workers (vendors, rickshaw pullers, construction), 234 (57%) worked through heatwave hours. Indicative pilot cost: Rs 3.8 crore over 2 years for 10 wards, two per city (Rs 38 lakh a ward).

Recommendation and the decision asked for in the opening lines; executive summary with cost, measure and timing; context with sourced data slots; a six-part ward plan; options table A-D with cost, implementer, feasibility and trade-off; six numbered recommendations with who, what, when and instrument; risks, next step, sources, method appendix; Hindi one-page summary in natural official Hindi; fact and judgement labelled. Ahmedabad 2013 heat action plan and the NDMA heat-wave guidelines are correct references. All figures are placeholders and the text is 1,437 words (under the 1,500 floor) because the brief claims the NGO's data is supplied but gives none. Policy rewrites that turn legal drafts into plain language
Onboarding summaries and policy FAQs for employees
Contractor, intern and vendor codes of conduct

Customer-facing terms and privacy policies: those are legal documents for a lawyer to draft
Announcing a policy change: write a genre:internal_memo that links to the policy
Publishing without legal review: a writer drafts and simplifies; a lawyer or HR-compliance specialist signs off

buyers: HR heads at startups and SMEs
cards.value_why: Upwork lists employee handbooks and company policies among business-writing projects (2026-01-21). Every growing Indian company needs one, and plain-language rewrites of lawyer drafts are recurring work.
cards.goal: An employee knows exactly what is expected, what they are entitled to, and whom to contact, without asking HR.

structure.does: Policy name, number and version, effective date, owner (role, not person), approval, next review date.
Why the policy exists, in one or two plain sentences.
Who it applies to (employees, interns, contractors, locations) and what it does not cover.
Only the terms used in the policy, defined in plain words, used consistently afterwards.
Numbered rules, one rule per clause, using 'must', 'may' and 'will' consistently, with numbers (days, amounts, times) stated.
How to apply, request, report or appeal: steps, forms, who approves, timelines.
What employees, managers, HR and any committee each do.
How exceptions are approved, what happens on breach (proportionate, with due process), and the escalation contact.
Links to related policies and laws, and the acknowledgement line.

length.note: A single policy is usually 500-2,500 words; a full handbook for a 50-500 person company runs 8,000-20,000. Legal requirements and the number of locations drive length; plain language shortens it.

checklist: Does the header state the effective date, owner and version?
Does the scope say who is covered and who is not?
Is each clause one rule, numbered, with numbers (days, amounts, deadlines) written as numerals?
Are 'must', 'may' and 'will' used consistently, with no 'shall/should' mix-ups?
Is there a clear procedure for requests, complaints or appeals, with timelines?
Is there a named escalation contact (role and channel)?
For a POSH policy: does it name the Internal Committee, how to file a complaint and the timelines, as reviewed by counsel?
If the policy covers monitoring or personal data, does it say what data is collected, why, and who sees it?
Has a lawyer or HR-compliance specialist reviewed it (marked in the hand-over note)?
pitfalls: Legalese copied from a template ('notwithstanding anything contained herein'): rewrite as 'Even if another policy says otherwise...'. Keep the legal meaning; have counsel confirm.
Rules without numbers ('reasonable notice', 'occasional WFH'): state '2 office days a week, Tuesday and Thursday' or '15 days' notice'.

Missing POSH basics: per the 2013 Act (secondary source), an Internal Committee is required at each office or branch with 10 or more employees, and employers must have a policy, run awareness programmes and file annual reports. Confirm current requirements with counsel before publishing.
Punitive tone ('Strict action will be taken'): state the specific consequence and the process, and add what support exists.
Monitoring clauses that hide what is collected: say exactly what (laptop activity, location, email), why and who can see it; data-protection duties under comp:dpdp_act_rules are phasing in.
No owner or review date: policies rot. Name the role that owns it and the next review date.
cards.exemplar_brief: Hybrid-work and attendance policy plus a one-page POSH policy summary for a 120-person Noida SaaS company's employee handbook; audience: all employees including interns and two remote contractors; English with key definitions repeated in Hindi; 1,200-1,800 words; numbered clauses, effective date, owner (Head of People), escalation contacts and Internal Committee details below; marked for legal review; goal: an employee knows how many office days are required, how to request an exception, and where to raise a complaint. Office-day rule: 3 days a week, Tuesday to Thursday, core hours 11 am-4 pm; interns follow the same rule; the two remote contractors are covered by their contracts, not the office-day rule. Exceptions: request through the HR portal at least 2 working days ahead; the manager decides within 1 working day; more than 4 exception days in a quarter need the Head of People's approval. Escalation: manager, then Head of People, then CEO. Internal Committee: Presiding Officer Kavita Sharma (senior woman employee), two employee members, one external member from an NGO; complaints to ic@brightside.example.

verified.note: 9/10. Header with version, effective date, owner, approval, review date and draft/legal-review status; purpose; scope covering interns and the remote contractors; Hindi definitions; numbered one-rule clauses with numerals; exception procedure with timelines; roles table; proportionate breach process with appeal; acknowledgements. cards.goal: Supporters repost or forward it with the source, and an undecided reader sees a fact they did not know.

structure.does: What happened, when and who said it, in one line, so the post makes sense out of context.
The opponent's claim stated fairly, quoted or closely paraphrased with attribution.
The number, date or document that answers it, with its source named (and a link or screenshot in the post or first reply).
What it means for the reader's life (fees, jobs, roads, prices), in plain words.
A short line that carries the argument on its own, often antithesis or a question.
For threads: one point per post, each with its own source, ending with a summary post.

length.note: Single posts run 25-80 words; threads 150-350. Platform limits (plat:x_post, plat:threads_post) and the forwarding habits of the audience decide.

checklist: Has the news peg been verified against a primary source (official release, video, document)?
Is the opponent's claim stated fairly, with attribution?
Does the counter-fact carry a number or date and a named source?
Does it attack policy or public record, not private life, caste, religion or community?
Is every allegation about a person either sourced or clearly framed as opinion?
Is any AI-generated or altered image, audio or video labelled?
Does the closing line work if it is the only line someone reads?
During an election period, has any paid or boosted version gone through MCMC pre-certification?
pitfalls: Posting on a forwarded screenshot that turns out to be fake or old: check the original source and date; a deleted post still gets screenshotted.

Personal attacks and private-life jibes: MCC norms bar criticism of private life and unverified allegations in campaigns, and defamation law (BNS s.356) protects good-faith opinion on public conduct, not invented imputations. Attack the record with a number.
Communal or caste framing: also an offence under BNS provisions on promoting enmity (comp:bns_defamation_speech) and an MCC violation. Frame around services, money and outcomes.
Unlabelled AI images or voice clones of leaders: India's 2026 IT Rules require prominent labels on realistic synthetic media, and ECI has issued directions on AI content in campaigns.
Numbers without a source ('lakhs of jobs'): name the figure, the year and the document; supporters need something to cite when challenged.
Misinformation tells ('forward as received', 'media won't show you this'): they cost credibility with undecided readers. Link the source instead.

Speeches in the legislature or at public hearings

Hosting and stage management: use genre:anchoring_script or genre:welcome_address_vote_of_thanks

cards.goal: The crowd repeats the slogan and leaves remembering the one ask (vote on the date for the symbol, join, turn out), and the clip that travels online carries the message.

structure.does: Greets leaders on stage and the crowd by place, in the local language or dialect; names a local landmark, hero or recent event.
One big contrast or question that frames the whole speech ('kal ka Saran, aaj ka Saran').
Local achievements with numbers and named places (roads, colleges, schemes), each tied to a person the crowd knows.
The opponent's record on the same issues, fact-based and public; policy and performance, not private life or community.
What happens next for this place, specific and believable; one promise per local issue.
Two or three short slogans placed at peaks, each repeated with the crowd; marked in the script.
One clear action: vote on the date, for the symbol, bring three people, join the booth team.
Return to the opening image or slogan, final chant.

length.note: Speaking slot decides: a 10-minute supporting speaker slot is short; a star campaigner's 30-40 minute address is long. Write to the slot and mark optional cuts.

checklist: Does the opening name the place and local people the crowd knows?
Is there one theme the whole speech returns to?
Is every achievement claim tied to a number and a named local place, supplied or verified by the campaign?
Does the contrast section stick to public record and policy, with no private-life attacks or unverified allegations?
Is it free of any appeal to vote on caste, religion or community?
Are 2-3 slogans marked for call-and-response, with pauses?
Is there exactly one ask, stated at least twice?
Is it written in the language and dialect the crowd speaks, in short sentences the speaker can say in one breath?
Are optional cuts marked so the speaker can shorten on stage?
pitfalls: A state-level speech pasted into every constituency: rewrite the local connect, record and promise sections for each place, with names the crowd knows.
Written Hindi ('Hamare dwara anek vikas karya sampann kiye gaye') instead of spoken Hindi: 'Humne sadak banwayi, college khulwaya. Aapne dekha, aap gawah ho.' Read it aloud in the speaker's voice.
Statistics nobody can hold ('Rs 4,327.6 crore'): round and localise: 'Rs 4,300 crore, that is Rs X for every family in this district' (only with campaign-verified numbers).
Personal or communal attacks that become the news clip: they breach the MCC and can attract BNS offences; contrast on record and services instead.
No pauses for the crowd: mark '(pause, slogan)' after peaks; a rally speech is a call-and-response, not a lecture.
Ending without a single ask: say what to do, when and for which symbol, twice.

Good write-ups lead with the outcome and the person's exact role, show why decisions were made rather than only final frames, credit collaborators, and respect client NDAs.

UX case studies for product designers' portfolios
Agency credentials decks that tell one project per page
Job applications where a hiring manager asks for two or three case studies
Award entries rewritten as portfolio pages after the result

A formal award submission with the jury's criteria: use genre:award_entry
Posting client work you do not have the right to show: check the contract, NDA and any employer rules on public posts first; anonymise or ask

cards.goal: A hiring manager or client understands what this person did, how they think, and shortlists them.

structure.does: Project name plus one line with what was made, for whom, and the result ('30-second Diwali film made in 10 days with an AI pipeline; 2.1M views').
Role, team size, timeline, tools, client (or 'regional jewellery brand' under NDA).
What was asked and what made it hard: budget, deadline, technical limit, audience.
The research finding or idea that set the direction, and why it fit the constraint.
Two to four key decisions, each with options considered, what was chosen and why, shown with captioned process images.
Hero visuals or video with captions that point out what to notice.
Metrics, client response, awards, or an honest qualitative outcome; only numbers the creator can back up.
What you would do differently, and every collaborator credited by role.

length.note: Visual-heavy Behance pages sit at 300-700 words; UX case studies with research run 800-1,500. Hiring managers skim: the outcome line and snapshot carry most of the weight.

checklist: Does the first line state what was made, for whom, and the result?
Is the creator's exact role stated (not 'we did everything')?
Is the main constraint named?
Are at least two decisions explained with the options considered and the reason for the choice?
Do process images have captions saying what to notice?
Is every metric one the creator can back up?
Are all collaborators credited by role?
Has client confidentiality been respected (NDA checked, names anonymised where needed)?
For AI-assisted work, is the human contribution and the tool pipeline stated plainly?
pitfalls: Gallery with no story (six final frames and 'Client: X'): hiring managers want decisions. Add the constraint and two decisions with reasons.
Claiming the team's work as yours ('I created the campaign'): name your role ('art direction and the generation pipeline; edit by Riya Shah').
Process theatre (every sticky note and persona) without the decision it led to: show only process that changed the outcome.
Vague results ('received great feedback'): give the number or the client's actual words, with permission.
Posting client or employer work without checking the contract: some contracts restrict public posts of work; check first, anonymise, or ask in writing.
Hiding AI use: state the pipeline and what you directed; buyers increasingly ask, and copyright protection depends on human authorship (comp:us_copyright_ai_authorship).

Tools: Midjourney for look development, Kling image-to-video, After Effects for compositing, DaVinci Resolve for grade. Decisions: (1) keep the jewellery real, using the brand's product stills composited into generated settings, not generating the pieces; (2) lock the look with a 12-frame reference board and one colour palette instead of prompting shot by shot; (3) cut hero shots from 14 to 9 and spend the saved days on regenerating hands and faces. Results, from the brand's report dated Friday 14 November 2025: 412,000 views and 9,800 saves on Instagram in 14 days (2.4% save rate). Client's written feedback: 'It felt like our showroom at night. We want her again for the wedding season.'

Outcome line first, exact role, snapshot, the named constraint, a sharp approach ('the generator as a location and lighting department, and the product as fixed'), three decisions with options and reasons, 8 captions that say what to notice, AI pipeline and human contribution stated, NDA respected, no invented metrics or tools. cards.name: Positioning statement / value proposition
cards.summary: One internal statement of who the product is for, what it is, the value it delivers and why it beats the alternative the customer would otherwise use, backed by the inputs and proof behind it. It is not public copy: taglines, homepage heroes and ads are written from it. Good statements name a specific best-fit customer, a real competitive alternative and a differentiator the team can prove.
use_for: Startup and product launches before any homepage or ad copy is written
Repositioning an existing product that is losing to a new alternative
Aligning founders, sales and the agency on one sentence
Brand strategy decks and messaging frameworks (the top line)
Value propositions for a single feature or plan
avoid: Public-facing lines: write genre:tagline_slogan or the hero of genre:homepage_copy from this statement
The full message hierarchy with pillars and proof per audience: use genre:messaging_framework
A person's positioning: use genre:personal_brand_statement
Mission and values: use genre:mission_vision_values

cards.goal: The team agrees on one sentence that decides what every public line, sales call and feature page says, and what it does not say.

structure.does: One line each: competitive alternatives (what customers use today, including spreadsheets or doing nothing), unique attributes, the value those attributes enable, best-fit customers, and the market category that makes the value obvious.
For [best-fit customer] who [need or job], [product] is a [category] that [key value]. Unlike [primary alternative], [product] [differentiator].
The facts that make the differentiator believable: data, customers, mechanism, guarantees.
Audiences, features or categories deliberately left out, so copywriters do not drift.
A first hero line and one-line pitch written from the statement, to test that it produces usable copy.

length.note: The statement itself is 35-70 words; inputs, proof and exclusions bring the deliverable to 150-300. Longer means it has become a messaging framework.

checklist: Does it name a specific best-fit customer, not 'businesses' or 'everyone'?
Does it name the real alternative customers use today (including manual work or doing nothing)?
Is the category one a buyer would recognise?
Is the differentiator something competitors cannot also claim?
Is there at least one proof point for the differentiator?
Is it free of buzzwords (world-class, innovative, seamless, one-stop)?
Can a copywriter write a homepage hero from it without asking a question?
Is anything deliberately excluded stated?
pitfalls: Naming a competitor nobody in the market compares you with: interview 5-10 recent buyers and ask what they used before; that is the alternative.

Differentiators everyone claims ('easy to use', 'affordable', 'great support'): find the attribute only you have and the value it unlocks: 'reminders go out on WhatsApp in Tamil from the pharmacy's own number'.
Writing the positioning statement as a tagline and publishing it: it is an internal tool; the public line is written from it.
Category confusion ('AI-powered omnichannel engagement platform'): pick the category the buyer already budgets for, or say plainly what new category you are creating and why.
Claims in the statement that later appear in ads without proof: comparative or factual claims must be substantiated under ASCI and CCPA rules; keep the proof points with the statement.

Client facts (demo data for this test; company invented): product Marundhu Mate. Messages go out from the pharmacy's own WhatsApp Business number. Pilot: 14 independent pharmacies in Coimbatore and Tiruppur, 8 weeks. Refill on time (within 3 days of the due date) among repeat customers rose from 31% to 44% against the pharmacies' own baseline (+13 points). Each pharmacy saved about 6 hours a week previously spent on manual reminder calls.

Dunford inputs in order, a 58-word Moore statement naming both real alternatives with a distinct differentiator for each, proof slots, sharp exclusions (no health-outcome or adherence claims, which keeps later ads inside ASCI and CCPA substantiation), and derived hero and pitch lines a copywriter can use; no buzzwords. The value clause is a feature (sends a WhatsApp message) more than the outcome, and the hero implies messages come from the pharmacy's own number, which the brief does not state. cards.name: Post-purchase / review request email
cards.summary: The emails after an order: thank-you and what happens next, how to use or care for the product, an honest review request once the customer has used it, and a cross-sell or replenishment timed to the product's use cycle. Good post-purchase emails help first and sell second, ask for reviews without steering them positive, and send marketing only to customers who opted in.

Review and photo-review requests
How-to-use, care and onboarding emails for physical products
Replenishment reminders for consumables (coffee, skincare, pet food)
Cross-sell emails for matching or next-step products
avoid: Order confirmations and shipping notices that are purely transactional: use genre:transactional_email (keep marketing out of them)
First emails after a sign-up with no purchase: use genre:welcome_email_series
Customers who stopped buying months ago: use genre:winback_email
Offering a discount or gift only for positive reviews (fake-review rules)

cards.goal: The customer uses the product well, leaves an honest review, and places a second order.

structure.does: Sent right after the order: thanks in a human voice, what happens next and when, where to track, who to contact. No upsell in the transactional part.

structure.part: Email 2: how to use or care
structure.does: Sent on dispatch or delivery: the 2-4 things that make the first use go right, with a short video or guide link.

Sent after enough time to use the product: asks for an honest review (and a photo), one tap to the form, says how reviews help other buyers. Any incentive is offered for any review, not a good one, and disclosed.
Timed to the product's use cycle, only to customers who consented to marketing: one relevant product or a refill reminder with a reason.
Subject + preheader pair, an opening line about their order, one job per email, one CTA button, sign-off from a named person.

length.note: Per email. A flow is 3-5 emails; timing depends on delivery time and how long the product takes to show results (coffee: days; skincare: weeks).

checklist: Does each email do one job with one CTA?
Is the review request sent only after the customer could have used the product?
Does the review request ask for an honest review, with no reward tied to a positive rating?
If an incentive is offered, is it for any review and disclosed?
Do cross-sell emails go only to customers who consented to marketing?
Does the subject line say what the email is about (no fake 'Re:' or 'Order issue')?
Is it signed by a named person with a way to reply?
Is the care or how-to content specific to this product (quantities, times, do-nots)?
pitfalls: Review gating ('Loved it? Leave 5 stars! Not happy? Email us instead'): steering only happy customers to public reviews and buying positive reviews fall foul of fake-review rules (comp:ftc_consumer_reviews_rule). Ask everyone the same way.
Review request the day after dispatch: the customer has not used it. Time it to delivery plus use (bedsheet: about 10 days; skincare: 3-4 weeks).

Treating a purchase as marketing consent: India's DPDP framework requires purpose-specific consent, and a purchase is not consent to marketing (comp:dpdp_act_rules). Send cross-sell only to opted-in customers.
'Dear valued customer' from noreply@: use the first name and a real person's sign-off that accepts replies.
Upsell crammed into the order confirmation: keep transactional emails transactional; sell in a separate, later email.
Fake subject lines ('Re: your order', 'Problem with your delivery') to lift opens: misleading headers break CAN-SPAM for US lists and trust everywhere.

ban.label: review gating or paid positive review

cards.exemplar_brief: Review-request email (email 3 of a 4-email post-purchase flow, sent on day 10 after delivery) for a Jaipur block-print bedsheet D2C brand; audience: women aged 28-50 in metros who bought their first sheet from the brand; English with one Hinglish line allowed; 80-150 words plus subject line and preheader; asks every customer the same way for an honest review with a photo, one tap to the form, signed by the founder, no reward tied to the rating; goal: an honest review with a photo.

Subject (41 characters) says what the email is, the preheader pairs with it, the opening ties to the order and day 10, one job and one CTA, the same honest-review ask for everyone with a reason and a photo request, no incentive and no gating, a natural Hinglish line ('Jo bhi lage, seedha likhiye. Humein sach sunna hai.'), founder sign-off. Only gap: no line inviting a direct reply, which the card's named-person-with-a-way-to-reply rule asks for.

cards.name: Product requirements document (PRD)
cards.summary: The document that defines the problem, users, goals and requirements of a product or feature so design and engineering can build it: problem with evidence, goals and non-goals, users and use cases, prioritised testable requirements, success metrics, constraints, launch plan and open questions. Good PRDs make the problem and the success measure unmissable, keep requirements testable, and say what is out of scope.
use_for: New feature or product definitions at startups and product companies
Alignment documents before design sprints or engineering estimates
Agency and outsourced builds where the client must sign off scope
One-page feature briefs that grow into full PRDs
Writing up requirements from founder interviews for a non-technical founder
avoid: How the system will be built (architecture, APIs, data models): use genre:technical_design_doc
Announcing what shipped: use genre:release_notes
Writing every requirement up front for an agile team: in agile, requirements start at a higher level for prioritisation and are detailed at the start of each cycle (Wikipedia)
UI copy itself: hand to genre:ux_microcopy once flows exist

sources.title: Wikipedia: Product requirements document
sources.supports: typical PRD components (purpose and scope, stakeholders, use cases, requirements, assumptions, constraints, dependencies, milestones, evaluation metrics); in agile, requirements start at a higher level and are elaborated each cycle

buyers: Product managers (writing it as part of the job)
cards.value_why: Written by product managers as part of the job rather than bought from freelancers; demand shows up as a skill in PM hiring, not as a marketplace category (PCW harvest). Freelance work exists mainly for founders and agencies who need scope written down.
cards.goal: Design and engineering can estimate and start building without a clarifying meeting, and everyone agrees what success looks like and what is out of scope.

structure.does: Title, owner, status (draft, in review, approved), last updated, reviewers and links to designs and tickets.
The user problem with evidence (data, support tickets, interview quotes), who has it, and why now.
2-4 measurable goals, each with a metric, baseline and target, and how it will be measured.
What this release deliberately does not do, to stop scope creep.
Primary and secondary users and the main scenarios or user stories ('As a member, I want..., so that...').
Numbered, prioritised (must / should / could) requirements, each testable with acceptance criteria, including edge cases and error states.
Links to designs and the key states: happy path, empty, loading, error, permission denied.
Legal, technical, partner and timeline constraints; assumptions to validate; teams or vendors this depends on.
Phases, feature flags, rollout percentage, support and comms, rollback trigger.
Each question with an owner and a due date.

length.note: A small feature: 600-1,500 words; a new product area: 3,000-6,000. Team size, risk and how many teams depend on it drive length; link out to research instead of pasting it.

checklist: Is the user problem stated with evidence, not just a solution idea?
Does every goal have a metric, a baseline and a target?
Is there a non-goals section?
Is every requirement numbered, prioritised and testable (a QA engineer could write a test from it)?
Are error, empty and edge-case states covered for the main flows?
Are terms used consistently (one name per concept throughout)?
Do open questions each have an owner and a due date?
If the feature collects or uses personal data, does the PRD say what data, for what purpose and how consent is taken?
Is the status and last-updated date current?
pitfalls: Untestable requirements ('The checkout should be fast and intuitive'): write 'Mandate setup screen loads in under 2 seconds on a 4G connection; 90% of test users complete it without help' (targets agreed with the team).
Solution-first PRDs ('Build a UPI AutoPay button'): start from the problem and evidence ('38% of members lapse because they forget to renew'; use the client's real number).
No non-goals: every reviewer adds their wish. List what is out of this release.
One concept, three names (member, user, customer): pick one per concept and define it once.
Happy path only: list the failure states (mandate rejected, bank down, user cancels in the bank app) with the required behaviour.
A PRD written once and never updated: keep status and decisions current, or the team builds from a stale version.
cards.exemplar_brief: PRD for adding UPI AutoPay mandate setup to the monthly membership flow of a Pune fitness-studio booking app; audience: 2 engineers, 1 designer, QA and the studio-operations lead; English; 1,200-2,000 words with problem, 3 goals with baselines and targets, non-goals, 10-15 prioritised testable requirements, failure states (mandate rejected, bank decline, user cancels), launch plan and open questions with owners; goal: engineering can estimate and design can start without a meeting. Client data (demo data for this test; invented): 18,000 active monthly members across 42 studios, average plan Rs 2,400 a month, all renewed manually today. Lapse: 11% of members miss their renewal date each month (about 1,980), and 4% (about 720) do not return within 30 days. Baselines and targets to use: on-time renewal 89% to 95%; members with an AutoPay mandate 0% to 40% of renewing members within 90 days of launch; payment-failure support tickets 38 per 1,000 members a month to 25.

Header, defined terms used consistently, problem with evidence slots, 3 goals with metric, baseline, target and method plus a guardrail, 5 non-goals, 5 user stories, 15 numbered M/S/C requirements each with an acceptance test, all three briefed failure states, UX states, a DPDP-aware data requirement, constraints (RBI pre-debit notice and the no-extra-authentication limit stated correctly without the figure), phased flag rollout with rollback trigger, open questions with owners. Government or institutional media packs for a scheme or summit

Marketing copy with superlatives: journalists discard it; state facts with dates and sources
Numbers that differ from the latest press release or filing: reconcile before publishing

cards.goal: A journalist files an accurate story from the kit alone, and calls the named contact when they need a quote or a hard answer.

structure.does: One page of facts: what the company does in one line, founded, founders, HQ, team size, customers or users, funding, key numbers each with an 'as of' date.
The standard 'About [company]' paragraph used at the end of every release.
Short and long bio for each spokesperson, with name spellings, titles and pronunciation if useful.
Three messages, each with one or two proof points a journalist can verify.
The company or launch story: problem, approach, milestones, market context with sourced figures.
Dated milestones in order.
The questions a sharp reporter will ask, including the uncomfortable ones (safety, losses, layoffs, competition), with straight answers.
Logos, product and leadership photos, video, each with a caption, credit and usage note.
Named person, phone, email, languages and response time.

length.note: A startup launch kit runs 1,200-2,500 words across its parts; event and institutional kits with schedules and speaker bios run longer. Each part must work when downloaded on its own.

checklist: Does every number carry an 'as of' date and match the latest press release?
Is the one-line description of the company plain enough to paste into a news story?
Are names, titles and spellings consistent across all parts?
Does the FAQ answer at least two uncomfortable questions directly?
Is every photo captioned and credited, with usage rights stated?
Is there a named media contact with phone, email and response time?
Is it free of superlatives that are not backed by a source ('India's first', 'industry-leading')?
Are short and long bios provided for each spokesperson?
pitfalls: Marketing language ('revolutionary', 'game-changing', 'world-class'): journalists delete it. Replace with the fact behind the adjective: '150 km on one charge in ARAI testing' (only if the client has the certificate).

'India's first' or 'largest' claims without proof: reporters check, and unsubstantiated claims in promotional material can breach the CCPA misleading-ads guidelines. Cite the source or drop the claim.
Avoiding the obvious hard question (a past battery fire, a layoff, a lawsuit): reporters will ask anyway. Give a straight, approved answer in the FAQ.
Stale numbers: a fact sheet with last year's user count undermines the launch. Date every number and update the kit with each release.
No contact or a generic info@ address: name a person who answers within the news cycle.
Mixing up press kit and influencer media kit: if the client says 'media kit', ask whether it is for journalists or for brand partners.
